title: Mass and Capacity Grade 3: Grams, Kilograms, Millilitres & Litres + Free Quiz
meta_title: Mass and Capacity Grade 3 Guide + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Teach mass and capacity to Grade 3 with grams, kilograms, millilitres and litres, easy conversions, scale-reading tips and a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: A bag of sugar is a kilogram, a water bottle holds a litre. Here is how I teach mass and capacity to Grade 3 kids without the confusion, plus a quick quiz to check what they know.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a Grade 3 child a packet of biscuits and ask ‘how heavy is this?’ and you will often hear ‘a hundred’ — a hundred what, nobody is sure. That gap is exactly what mass and capacity for Grade 3 is meant to close: not just measuring, but knowing which unit the number belongs to. A slice of bread is measured in grams; a bag of atta in kilograms; the medicine spoon in millilitres; the cooking oil tin in litres. Get the child matching the object to the right unit and half the topic is already won.

In my experience teaching eight-year-olds, the mistakes are almost never with the arithmetic. They are with the sense of size — a child who writes that a school bag weighs 3 grams simply has not held enough real objects. So this is a hands-on chapter. Kitchen scales, an old measuring jug, a few water bottles: that is your whole toolkit.

The four units a Grade 3 child needs

Grade 3 keeps it to four units, two for mass and two for capacity. Mass tells you how heavy a thing is; capacity tells you how much liquid a container holds. Do not muddle capacity with weight — a big empty bucket has large capacity but very little mass.

MeasuresSmall unitBig unitEveryday example
Mass (how heavy)gram (g)kilogram (kg)a pencil is a few g; a watermelon is a few kg
Capacity (how much liquid)millilitre (ml)litre (l)a spoon of syrup is 5 ml; a milk packet is 1 l

The only two conversions to learn

The whole chapter rests on two facts, and they are beautifully similar:

  • 1 kg = 1000 g — one kilogram is one thousand grams.
  • 1 l = 1000 ml — one litre is one thousand millilitres.

Because both use 1000, a child who owns one owns both. To go from the big unit to the small unit you multiply by 1000 (so 2 kg = 2000 g, and 3 l = 3000 ml). To go the other way you divide by 1000. I teach the ‘big to small, times a thousand’ rule as a little chant, and it sticks.

Half and quarter tricks

Two half-values earn their keep because they turn up constantly in Indian kitchens and shops. Half a kilogram is 500 g — that is the classic ‘paav-kilo, aadha-kilo’ talk at the sabzi market. Half a litre is 500 ml, the size of a small cold-drink bottle. Once a child knows 500 g and 500 ml on sight, estimation gets far more confident.

Choosing the right unit

This is the skill that separates real understanding from rote answers. Before measuring anything, ask: is this heavy enough for kilograms, or should I use grams? Is this a jug-sized amount for litres, or a spoon-sized amount for millilitres? A quick rule of thumb I give my students:

  • Use grams for things lighter than a bag of atta — a chikoo, a chocolate bar, a letter.
  • Use kilograms for the heavier stuff — a school bag, a baby, a sack of rice.
  • Use millilitres for small pours — a dose of medicine, a glass of juice.
  • Use litres for the big containers — a bucket, a petrol tank, a cooking-oil tin.

Reading scales and measuring jugs

A kitchen scale and a measuring jug both work the same way: find the marks, then count the small steps between the big numbers. On a jug marked 0, 200, 400, 600 ml with four little lines between each big number, every small step is 50 ml. Children rush straight to the number without checking the step size, and that is the number-one error I correct. Slow down, work out what one small mark is worth, then read.

A genuine caveat here: not every scale is marked in tidy hundreds. Get your child used to reading a jug where the steps are 25 ml or 250 ml, not just friendly round numbers, or the first tricky exam question will throw them.

Adding and subtracting mass and capacity

Once the units and the reading are secure, the sums are ordinary Grade 3 arithmetic — you just keep the same unit throughout and write it at the end. If a bag holds 350 g of dal and you add 400 g more, you have 750 g. If a 2 l jug has 1 l 200 ml poured out, 800 ml is left. The trap is mixing units: you cannot add 1 kg to 200 g until both are in the same unit. Convert first (1 kg = 1000 g, so the total is 1200 g), then add. Same story for litres and millilitres.

Estimate first, then check

My favourite routine, and the one that builds real number sense, is estimate-then-check. Before you weigh the apple, guess: 100 g or 500 g? Before you fill the glass, guess: 200 ml or 2 litres? Then measure and see how close you were. Over a week of guessing-and-checking with real objects, a child stops writing ‘a school bag weighs 3 grams’ forever, because they have finally felt what a gram and a kilogram actually are. That felt sense is worth more than any memorised conversion.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a free 8-question quiz on grams, kilograms, millilitres, litres, the 1000 conversions and choosing the right unit — all at Grade 3 level. Let your child try it and read the explanations for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable worksheet at the end gives graded questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 3 Mass and Capacity Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on grams, kilograms, millilitres, litres and the 1000 conversions. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: Which unit would you use to measure how heavy a watermelon is?
questions.explanation: A watermelon is heavy, so we use kilograms (kg). Grams would need very large numbers.

questions.q: How many grams are there in 1 kilogram?
questions.explanation: 1 kg = 1000 g. To change kilograms to grams, multiply by 1000.
1 l = 1000 ml, the same 1000 pattern as kilograms and grams.

questions.q: Which unit is best for a spoon of cough syrup?
questions.explanation: A spoon holds a small amount of liquid, so we measure it in millilitres (ml).

questions.q: How much is 2 kg written in grams?
questions.explanation: Big unit to small unit means times 1000, so 2 kg = 2000 g.

questions.q: A jug has 350 ml of juice. You pour in 400 ml more. How much is in the jug now?
questions.explanation: Add the two amounts in the same unit: 350 ml + 400 ml = 750 ml.

questions.q: What is another way to write half a kilogram?
questions.explanation: Half of 1000 g is 500 g, so half a kilogram is 500 g.

questions.q: A bag holds 1 kg of rice and another holds 200 g. How much rice altogether?
questions.explanation: First make units match: 1 kg = 1000 g. Then 1000 g + 200 g = 1200 g.

faq.q: What is the difference between mass and capacity?
faq.a: Mass tells you how heavy an object is, measured in grams and kilograms. Capacity tells you how much liquid a container can hold, measured in millilitres and litres. An empty bucket has large capacity but small mass.

faq.q: What are the two conversions a Grade 3 child must remember?
faq.a: Just two, and both use 1000: 1 kg = 1000 g and 1 l = 1000 ml. Big unit to small unit means multiply by 1000; small unit to big unit means divide by 1000.

faq.q: How do I help my child choose the right unit?
faq.a: Compare the object to a bag of atta. Lighter than that, use grams; heavier, use kilograms. For liquids, spoon-sized amounts are millilitres and jug-sized amounts are litres. Practising with real kitchen objects fixes this fast.

faq.q: Why does my child read a measuring jug wrong?
faq.a: Almost always because they skip the step size. Between the big numbers on a jug are small marks — work out what one small mark is worth first, then count. If 0 to 200 ml has four gaps, each mark is 50 ml.
